questions.stem: Urea is 45 mg/100 mL in proximal tubular fluid and 15 mg/100 mL in blood. Permeability is 2×10⁻⁵ cm/s and area 100 cm². What is the urea flux?
questions.explanation: J = P·A·ΔC = (2×10⁻⁵ cm/s)(100 cm²)(30 mg/100 mL = 0.3 mg/cm³) = 6×10⁻⁴ mg/s, from higher (lumen) to lower (blood). A: Wrong direction. C: Uses 30 mg/cm³; forgets that 1 mL = 1 cm³ and the /100 mL. D: Uses the lumen concentration (45) instead of the difference. E: Drops the factor of 2 in P.
questions.source: Transport Across the Cell Membrane, slides 19–20

questions.stem: A transport process moves its solute downhill, shows saturation, transports D- but not L-glucose, and is unaffected by ouabain. Which process is it?
questions.explanation: Downhill, carrier-mediated (saturable, stereospecific), no energy → facilitated diffusion. B: Simple diffusion isn't saturable or stereospecific. C: Primary active transport moves solute uphill. D, E: Secondary active transport is uphill and is inhibited by ouabain (loss of the Na⁺ gradient).
questions.source: Transport Across the Cell Membrane, slides 12, 22, 28

questions.stem: In the intestinal epithelium, which pair of transporters accounts for transcellular glucose absorption?
questions.explanation: Apical SGLT uses the Na⁺ gradient (secondary active); basolateral GLUT2 lets glucose out by facilitated diffusion; the basolateral Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase maintains the gradient. A: Reversed. C: The pump is basolateral, but glucose entry needs SGLT to go uphill. D: NKCC1 and CFTR mediate Cl⁻ secretion. E: H⁺/K⁺-ATPase is the gastric parietal-cell pump.
questions.source: Transport Across the Cell Membrane, slide 49

questions.stem: Which epithelium is best suited to maintain a large transepithelial osmotic gradient?
questions.explanation: Tight epithelia maintain steep gradients, and the lecture names the urinary bladder as the tightest of all (claudins set paracellular permeability). A, B, E: Leaky epithelia do bulk, nearly isosmotic transport. C: The colon is tight, but less so than the bladder.
questions.source: Transport Across the Cell Membrane, slides 50–51

questions.stem: In the renal collecting tubule, Na⁺ enters through apical ENaC and is pumped out basolaterally. How is Cl⁻ absorbed with it?

options.C: Paracellularly, driven by a lumen-negative voltage
options.D: Paracellularly, driven by a lumen-positive voltage
options.E: Paracellularly, by solvent drag with water

questions.explanation: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump moves positive charge from lumen to interstitium, making the lumen negative; this drives passive Cl⁻ absorption across the tight junctions. A: There is no primary Cl⁻ pump in this model. B: NKCC2 is the thick ascending limb transporter. D: The lumen becomes negative, and a lumen-positive voltage would hold Cl⁻ in the lumen. E: Solvent drag is described for leaky epithelia like the proximal tubule.
questions.source: Transport Across the Cell Membrane, slides 55, 57

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man has LDL of 350 mg/dL and tendon xanthomas. His LDL receptors bind LDL normally but fail to internalize it. What is the most likely defect?

options.D: Receptor unable to cluster into clathrin-coated pits
options.E: Failure of receptor recycling from endosomes

questions.explanation: In this form of familial hypercholesterolemia the receptor binds LDL but can't enter clathrin-coated pits, so there is no receptor-mediated endocytosis. A: Receptors are present and bind. B: Binding is normal. C: Lipase deficiency acts after internalization. E: Recycling happens after internalization, which never occurs here.
questions.source: Transport Across the Cell Membrane, slides 39–41

questions.stem: A child with cystic fibrosis has thick airway mucus. Which step of airway NaCl secretion is defective?
questions.explanation: Cl⁻ loaded by NKCC1 exits apically via CFTR; the lumen-negative voltage then pulls Na⁺ paracellularly, and water follows. Without CFTR, secretion fails and mucus thickens. A, B: These basolateral steps are intact. C: ENaC mediates Na⁺ absorption, not secretion. D: Paracellular Na⁺ follows Cl⁻ passively; it isn't the primary defect.
questions.source: Transport Across the Cell Membrane, slides 56, 59

questions.stem: Histamine rapidly increases gastric acid secretion. By which type of regulation does it act on the parietal cell?

options.B: Recruitment of H⁺/K⁺-ATPase to the apical membrane
options.E: Inhibition of the pump by omeprazole

questions.explanation: Histamine translocates the H⁺/K⁺ pump to the apical membrane (recruitment of existing transporters). A: Increased synthesis is the aldosterone example (Na⁺/K⁺ pump subunits). C: Post-transcriptional modification is the CFTR example. D: Claudin modulation is the aldosterone/claudin-8 example. E: Omeprazole blocks the pump, lowering acid.
questions.source: Transport Across the Cell Membrane, slides 24, 59

questions.stem: Ouabain is applied to intestinal epithelium, and glucose absorption falls. Why?

options.A: SGLT loses the Na⁺ gradient that drives glucose entry
options.C: SGLT is a P-type ATPase that ouabain inhibits
options.D: Ouabain competes with glucose for SGLT
options.E: Tight junctions open and glucose leaks back

questions.explanation: Ouabain inhibits the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase; the Na⁺ gradient that powers secondary active SGLT transport collapses. B: GLUT2 isn't the ouabain target. C: SGLT is a cotransporter (secondary active), not an ATPase. D: Ouabain binds the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, not SGLT. E: Ouabain isn't described as acting on tight junctions.
questions.source: Transport Across the Cell Membrane, slides 24–25, 28, 49
